title: Transitions - Advanced
description: Full in-context questions with four options, plus why each distractor fails.

cards.front: 00 HOW · How this deck differs
cards.back: Deck 1 taught you what each transition MEANS. This deck makes you apply it under test conditions. | Every card gives you a real two-sentence context and four options, exactly like the test. | Say your own relationship phrase BEFORE you read the options. If you skip that step these get much harder.

cards.front: 01 CONTRAST vs ADDITION · 'Coral reefs recover from bleaching if the water cools within weeks. ___, repeated bleaching in consecutive years leaves them unable to rebuild.' A) Similarly B) However C) In addition D) For example
cards.back: B) However. | The second sentence REVERSES the hopeful first one, so you need contrast. | A fails: repeated bleaching is not parallel to recovery, it is opposed. C fails: this is not a second equal point, it is a reversal. D fails: it is not an instance of recovery.

cards.front: 01 CONTRAST vs ADDITION · 'The alloy resists corrosion in salt water. ___, it can be machined without specialized tooling.' A) Nevertheless B) In addition C) By contrast D) Therefore
cards.back: B) In addition. | Two separate POSITIVE properties, equally weighted. Pure addition. | A and C fail because nothing is being opposed. D fails because machinability is not caused by corrosion resistance.

cards.front: 01 CONTRAST vs ADDITION · 'Early maps placed the river's source in the western hills. ___, modern surveys trace it to a spring forty kilometers north.' A) Consequently B) For instance C) In fact D) By contrast
cards.back: D) By contrast. | Two comparable sources of information that DISAGREE. | C is tempting but 'in fact' would need to strengthen the first claim, and this overturns it. A fails: the new survey is not caused by the old map.

cards.front: 02 CAUSE vs ADDITION · 'The dam cut the river's sediment load by ninety percent. ___, the delta downstream began losing land within a decade.' A) Meanwhile B) As a result C) Likewise D) Admittedly
cards.back: B) As a result. | The land loss is the OUTCOME of the sediment cut. Direct causation. | A fails: these are not simultaneous unrelated events, one caused the other. C fails: they are not parallel situations.

cards.front: 02 CAUSE vs ADDITION · 'Every sample from the three sites shared an identical isotope signature. ___, they must all originate from a single quarry.' A) Therefore B) Similarly C) However D) Specifically
cards.back: A) Therefore. | The second sentence is a CONCLUSION DEDUCED from the first. | D fails because the conclusion is new information, not a sharpening of the same claim. B fails because nothing is being compared.

cards.front: 02 CAUSE vs ADDITION · 'Trials showed the initial dosage produced severe side effects in a third of participants. ___, the researchers halved it before the second phase.' A) Consequently B) Accordingly C) Nevertheless D) In other words
cards.back: B) Accordingly. | Someone TOOK ACTION in response, which is exactly what 'accordingly' marks. | A is close and would not be wrong in isolation, but 'accordingly' is preferred when an agent acts deliberately. This A-vs-B distinction is the hard part of this question type.

cards.front: 03 EXAMPLE vs SPECIFICATION · 'Some plants outsource their defense to insects. ___, acacia trees house colonies of stinging ants inside hollow thorns.' A) Specifically B) For example C) In addition D) Indeed
cards.back: B) For example. | The acacia is a STANDALONE INSTANCE of the general rule. That is the strict test for 'for example'. | A would be right if the sentence merely narrowed the same claim, but it introduces a separate case.

cards.front: 03 EXAMPLE vs SPECIFICATION · 'The decline did not affect the whole population equally. ___, it was confined almost entirely to birds nesting on the ground.' A) For example B) Specifically C) Nevertheless D) Similarly
cards.back: B) Specifically. | The second sentence SHARPENS the same claim rather than giving a separate case. | A fails because ground-nesting birds are not an instance of 'unequal decline', they are the precise content of it. This is the single most tested distinction.

cards.front: 03 EXAMPLE vs SPECIFICATION · 'Several early photographers experimented with paper negatives. ___, Talbot's calotype process produced images from a waxed paper sheet.' A) In particular B) Therefore C) Conversely D) In summary
cards.back: A) In particular. | Singles out ONE member of a group already named. | 'For example' would also be defensible, which is your signal that neither is the intended answer here; 'in particular' is stronger because Talbot is presented as the notable case.

cards.front: 04 CONCESSION · 'The core sample was small, poorly preserved, and collected without modern controls. ___, it remains the only physical evidence from the period.' A) Therefore B) Nevertheless C) Furthermore D) In other words
cards.back: B) Nevertheless. | The first sentence CONCEDES weaknesses; the second asserts value anyway. Textbook concession. | C fails because it would add another weakness, not push back. A reverses the logic entirely.

cards.front: 04 CONCESSION · 'The model tracks the last forty years of data almost exactly. ___, it fails badly for any year before 1960.' A) That said B) Consequently C) Likewise D) For this reason
cards.back: A) That said. | Grants the strength, then introduces the limitation. | B and D both require causation, and the pre-1960 failure is not caused by the recent accuracy. C requires parallel likeness.

cards.front: 04 CONCESSION · 'Only two of the eleven trials reached significance. ___, the direction of the effect was identical in all eleven.' A) Regardless B) Admittedly C) Indeed D) Still
cards.back: D) Still. | Concedes the weak significance, then holds onto a genuine finding. | A dismisses the prior point as irrelevant, but here it IS relevant and is being weighed. B would introduce the concession, not answer it. This A-vs-D pair is a common trap.

cards.front: 05 RESTATEMENT TRAP · 'The species has never been recorded outside this single valley. ___, it is found nowhere else on Earth.' A) However B) In other words C) For example D) As a result
cards.back: B) In other words. | The second sentence genuinely RESTATES the first with zero new information. This is the rare case where it is correct. | Note how strict the condition is: if the sentence added even one new fact, B would be wrong.

cards.front: 05 RESTATEMENT TRAP · 'The valve does not settle into a single position. ___, it opens and closes roughly once per second.' A) In other words B) Instead C) Nevertheless D) Moreover
cards.back: B) Instead. | Something was NEGATED, then replaced with what actually happens. That is 'instead', not restatement. | A is the trap: the oscillation is NEW information, not a rephrasing. Students pick A here constantly.

cards.front: 05 RESTATEMENT TRAP · 'The pigment is not derived from crushed lapis, as collectors long assumed. ___, it is a synthetic copper compound first made in the 1820s.' A) In other words B) Rather C) Similarly D) In addition
cards.back: B) Rather. | A negation followed by the correction. 'Rather' is built for exactly this. | A fails because the copper compound is new content. 'Instead' would also work, which tells you the test would only offer one of them.

cards.front: 06 EMPHASIS vs ADDITION · 'The technique is not a modern invention. ___, it is described in a printer's manual published in 1740.' A) In fact B) Moreover C) Similarly D) Nevertheless
cards.back: A) In fact. | CONFIRMS the claim and then strengthens it with something surprising. | B fails because the 1740 manual is not a second separate point; it is the evidence that makes the first claim vivid.

cards.front: 06 EMPHASIS vs ADDITION · 'The effect is not subtle. ___, it appeared in every one of the ninety trials without exception.' A) Indeed B) In addition C) For example D) By contrast
cards.back: A) Indeed. | Affirms and INTENSIFIES: the second sentence goes further than the first. | C is the trap, but ninety-of-ninety is not one instance, it is the full strength of the claim.

cards.front: 07 SEQUENCE · 'The site is now dated to roughly 9,000 years ago. ___, archaeologists had confidently assigned it to the Bronze Age.' A) Subsequently B) Previously C) Meanwhile D) Ultimately
cards.back: B) Previously. | The second sentence looks BACKWARD to an earlier belief. | A points forward and reverses the chronology, which is the intended error. Watch the tense: 'had assigned' is your clue.

cards.front: 07 SEQUENCE · 'The northern crew drilled through the ice shelf for six weeks. ___, a second team surveyed open water two hundred kilometers south.' A) Afterward B) Meanwhile C) Consequently D) Therefore
cards.back: B) Meanwhile. | Two things happening SIMULTANEOUSLY in different places. | A makes them sequential, which the passage does not support. C and D require causation.

cards.front: 07 SEQUENCE · 'The wetland once covered forty square kilometers. ___, it covers fewer than five.' A) Currently B) Eventually C) Previously D) Finally
cards.back: A) Currently. | Contrasts the PRESENT state against the past. 'Once' in the first sentence demands a present-tense counterpart. | C would double the backward reference. B implies a completed process rather than a present state.

cards.front: 08 PURPOSE · 'The city set out to lower summer street temperatures by four degrees. ___, it planted twelve thousand shade trees over three years.' A) To that end B) As a result C) In addition D) Nevertheless
cards.back: A) To that end. | An explicit GOAL is stated, then the ACTION taken to reach it. | B is the near-miss: the planting is not a consequence of having a goal, it is the method chosen to achieve it. That distinction is the whole question.

cards.front: 08 PURPOSE · 'Older cores may have been contaminated during decades of uncontrolled storage. ___, the team re-sampled every site from scratch.' A) With this in mind B) Similarly C) In fact D) Regardless
cards.back: A) With this in mind. | Acts on the CONSIDERATION just raised. | D is tempting because it sounds decisive, but 'regardless' would mean they re-sampled while IGNORING the contamination risk, which inverts the logic.

cards.front: 09 SIMILARITY TRAP · 'Coral bleaches when water rises past a narrow temperature threshold. ___, kelp forests collapse above a similarly tight limit.' A) Likewise B) However C) Consequently D) In other words
cards.back: A) Likewise. | Two genuinely PARALLEL systems behaving the same way. This is the rare case where a similarity word is correct. | Note what makes it work: both halves describe the same mechanism in different organisms.

cards.front: 09 SIMILARITY TRAP · 'Desert soils lose nitrogen within a single season. ___, wetland soils can hold it for decades.' A) Similarly B) By contrast C) In addition D) Specifically
cards.back: B) By contrast. | The two soils behave OPPOSITELY, so the parallel structure demands a contrast word, not a similarity word. | A is the trap: the sentences are parallel in FORM but opposite in CONTENT. Form parallelism fools students into picking 'similarly'.

cards.front: 10 DISMISSAL TRAP · 'The construction permits were filed almost three weeks late. ___, ground was broken on the originally scheduled date.' A) Nevertheless B) Regardless C) Therefore D) Consequently
cards.back: A) Nevertheless. | The late filing is a real obstacle that is being CONCEDED and then overcome. | B is the trap and it is subtle: 'regardless' would treat the late permits as IRRELEVANT, but the sentence's whole point is that they mattered and were overcome anyway.

cards.front: 11 MULTI-STEP · 'Warmer springs cause insects to hatch earlier. ___, migrating birds arrive to find their food supply already past its peak.' A) In turn B) Similarly C) Meanwhile D) Admittedly
cards.back: A) In turn. | A CHAIN: warmth causes early hatching, which then causes the birds' problem. 'In turn' marks the second link. | C fails because these are sequential consequences, not simultaneous events.

cards.front: 11 MULTI-STEP · 'She rewrote the routine to use only integer arithmetic. ___, she cut its runtime by more than half.' A) In doing so B) Therefore C) Additionally D) For example
cards.back: A) In doing so. | The ACTION ITSELF produced the effect, and the same agent does both. | B is defensible in isolation but weaker: 'in doing so' ties the result directly to the act described, which is what the sentence structure signals.

cards.front: 12 REGISTER · 'The proposed route is eighty kilometers longer than the existing one. ___, no one has surveyed the terrain on the far side of the pass.' A) Besides B) What's more C) Moreover D) In addition
cards.back: D) In addition. | Two separate practical objections of comparable weight. | A and B are correct in MEANING but far too informal for the test's register. C implies escalation, and an unsurveyed route is not obviously a bigger problem than the extra distance. Register decides this one.

cards.front: 12 REGISTER · 'First, the chronology does not match the geology. ___, no second sample was ever collected for comparison.' A) Secondly B) Second C) Lastly D) In the second place
cards.back: B) Second. | The test prefers 'second' to 'secondly' and to 'in the second place'. | A and D are the same meaning in the wrong register. C would require this to be the final item, which nothing establishes.

cards.front: 13 HARD PAIR · 'Basalt weathers far more rapidly than granite does. ___, geologists rely on it to date recent lava flows.' A) For this reason B) Nevertheless C) In comparison D) Specifically
cards.back: A) For this reason. | Points explicitly BACK at the stated cause (rapid weathering) to explain the practice. | C is the trap: the first sentence does contain a comparison, but the second sentence is a CONSEQUENCE of it, not a further comparison.

cards.front: 13 HARD PAIR · 'The manuscript is unmistakably a working draft rather than a finished text. ___, its contradictions and false starts are expected rather than puzzling.' A) As such B) However C) For instance D) Likewise
cards.back: A) As such. | 'Because of the quality just described' - the draft status is what makes the contradictions unsurprising. | B inverts it. C fails because contradictions are not an instance of draft-ness, they are its consequence.

cards.front: 13 HARD PAIR · 'Three independent teams attempted a full reconstruction of the sequence. ___, the simplest of the competing models proved correct.' A) Ultimately B) Consequently C) Meanwhile D) In conclusion
cards.back: A) Ultimately. | Names the FINAL upshot after a process. | B fails because the simple model's correctness was not caused by three teams trying. D rarely fits on this test, because passages are excerpts rather than finished essays.

cards.front: 14 NO-TRANSITION CASE · When the answer adds no connector
cards.back: Occasionally the credited answer is the option that simply continues the sentence with no logical connector at all, or with a bare word like 'there' or 'then'. | If every relationship word feels forced, check whether the sentences are simply sequential narration. | Do not manufacture a relationship the passage does not have.

cards.front: 14 STRATEGY · The two-pass method for transition questions
cards.back: PASS 1: decide AGREE or DISAGREE, and cross out the two options on the wrong side. Ten seconds. | PASS 2: between the two survivors, ask which one's strict condition is actually met (does it need a concession? an instance? a restatement with no new info?). | You will get most of these right without ever feeling clever.

cards.front: 14 STRATEGY · What to do when two options survive
cards.back: Ask which one demands MORE of the passage. The test rewards the option whose conditions are exactly met, not the one that is merely compatible. | 'For example' demands a standalone instance. 'In other words' demands zero new information. 'Nevertheless' demands a genuine concession. | If a condition is only half met, that option is wrong.
